title: Larry away, the Society's dispute, and taking over the bands in September 1961
summary: While Borenstein was away getting married the Society tried to run the hall and lost money; Jaffe then took over booking, moving to nightly, six-night union-rate concerts.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: Well, can you... Well, what we were saying before is you told him about when, you know, the whole thing... So the whole thing actually took place, you know, in a couple weeks that... In a couple weeks that, uh, you know, Larry was away. Well, not... The Society was founded, and, you know... Oh, he was on that one, he was away. Yeah, well, he went to get married. Yeah. And... It was in that time that... The Society only, you know, I don't think lasted a month. Did it? No. No. So I'm saying it must have been going for two weeks while Larry was away. And two weeks after he came back. Okay. And that was it. Well, can you tell me about this time that there was a sort of a transfer of power, you might say, in the hall when... Because originally, or initially, I believe Ken Mills was, as you say, sort of hiring a band. Yeah. And Larry went away. And Larry went away. Yeah. And also... Also making up the difference, you know, because... Yeah. At that time, band was just under a... Oh, of course, about 90... 93. 50, 92. 59. And, you know, we weren't... I would say that one of the weekend nights, you know, that they were making it, you know, that they were making it, you know, that they were making it, you know, and they were making it up to carry, you know, maybe cover up the deficit of two days, maybe, but they weren't, you know, it was not... Every week was running into a deficit. Yeah. Wow. So... Now, then he went... Larry went away, and there's some story about how... Anyway, you can tell him the story. Then Larry came back and said he got mad or something. Yeah. Well, he's, you know, he was mad. He was mad, first of all, because, you know, that, uh, you know, when he told him, this, I was, you know, the society says, you know, and, you know, he, like, you know, at first refused to, you know, you know, admit, you know, that there was, you know, such an organization. And, uh, everybody in the thing itself, you know, you know, sort of, sort of hassled. Uh, the minute there was an organization, you know, they wanted to schedule bands, you know, say, well, you know, I like this band, and, uh, people said, well, there was another group that said the leader should bring, you know, who he wants to bring, and another one said, you know, Ken felt, you know, that he wanted to, you know, pick the personnel. And, uh. Well, when, when did you take over the business of having bands, and generally running hall, as you do now, more or less? September. September of 61? Yeah. June, July, August. Yeah. The hall went for just about three months. Yeah. And it was running continuous, the whole life. Yeah. And it was running continuous. Yeah. How did you say that? It was running, were you running every night? It was running five, six nights a week, five nights a week a start. Well, we started off, you know, three nights a week, four nights a week a week, and, you know, I think we were running four nights a week when, you know, when the union said that it would give us a better rate if we went, you know, six nights a week. We went six nights a week. And sometimes one of the nightly concerts would be on a Sunday afternoon instead. It wasn't, you know, I mean, it was the hours of Chang, we used to run, oh, the one they finally settled on was eight to twelve. But there are other times that it ran, you know, earlier and later. We had schedules from those days. I know. I've got some of those fairly early schedules. I haven't got any of those fairly early ones, you know, whether they're not living out. We used to make them on a Jell-O, you know, on those Jell-O transfer plates. Remember? Yeah. Do you, um... That was when the Society was still going. To what extent have you been able to keep records, actually, over the years, of people who were playing at Preservation Hall? Well, we published a list one time. They were put in the back of a program or something. Some of the other schedules or something. Yeah. And... Um... So I don't know, you know, who was here necessarily on any given day, you know. A friend of mine came down here actually at that time and around about, I think it was around August of 61, and he, for many of you, of course, was very excited and he got back. All the bands for about two weeks. I know who else was here. A Japanese kid did the same thing. What's that? With a hearing aid. Oh, yeah. Uh, you know, Hero and a Mac. Yeah. Well, um, yeah, he was here. He was here from the very beginning. He must have been, you know, a member of the Society. How, uh, at the beginning of that you were charging, uh, just donations? Well, when it started, we had, we used to use the door behind the piano as the main entrance. Um, people came in there and we moved the band from the back of the room to the front of the room, pretty much once this concert started. There was a lot of argument about that, a lot of people. You know, these things were not just something that, you know, an argument about that would be a major meeting and, you know, everybody would... Uh, people, you wouldn't even ask people for money when they came in. No. You asked, you would, you would pass the kiddie.
